title: Four Rooms in One County
bigQuestion: What can the name, the rules and the rent of a training room tell us about where a martial art came from?

story.title: Four Doors on One Strip
story.kicker: A family looking for an after-school class finds four signs with four words for school.
paragraphs: Maya rides in the back seat along a busy road in an Illinois county. Her family is looking for an after-school class. They pull into a row of shops with one long parking lot. There is a pizza place, a phone store and a laundromat. Between them are four doors with sports signs.

The first sign says Karate Dojo. The second says Taekwondo Dojang. The third says Boxing Gym in big red letters. The fourth says Judo Club, with a small picture of a white jacket. Maya reads them out loud. "Why does every one use a different word for school?" she asks.

Her mother points at the windows. Inside the dojo, students in white line up by belt color. Inside the dojang, the flag of South Korea hangs beside the flag of the United States. Inside the gym, a square ring with ropes fills the back half of the room.

Maya's older brother wrestles for the high school. His room has no sign on any street. It sits down a hallway past the cafeteria, with mats from wall to wall and a list of weight classes taped by the door. "That makes five rooms," he says. "And each one answers to a different rule book."
story.think: Why might four schools on one strip choose four different words for the same idea?

lessons.title: Dojo: Place of the Way
lessons.mainIdea: Dojo is a Japanese word for a training hall, and it first named a place of Buddhist practice.
reading: The Japanese word *dojo* is written with two characters. The first means "way" or "path." The second means "place." So a dojo is a "place of the way." The same first character appears in judo, "the gentle way," and in kendo, "the way of the sword."

The word is older than any sport. Buddhist writers in China and Japan used it for the spot where the Buddha reached awakening. Later it named temple halls used for meditation and study. Over the centuries, Japanese sword and archery schools also called their training halls dojo.

In 1882, Kanō Jigorō opened his judo school at Eishō-ji. It was a Buddhist temple in Tokyo. He named it the *Kodokan*, meaning a hall for teaching the way. An Illinois storefront with a dojo sign borrows that long history.

words.d: a Japanese word for a training hall; it means "place of the way"
the judo school Kanō Jigorō founded in Tokyo in 1882; still the world center of judo

look.title: A Sign in Two Languages
look.text: Picture a storefront window. Large English letters read "Karate Dojo." Below them, two Japanese characters are painted in black. A newer sign next door reads "Martial Arts Academy" with no Japanese words at all.
look.prompt: What might each owner want families to understand from the sign they chose?

check.q: What does the Japanese word dojo mean, part by part?
check.why: Dojo joins the characters for way and place, so it means place of the way.

check.q: Where did Kanō Jigorō open the Kodokan in 1882?
choices: at Eishō-ji, a Buddhist temple in Tokyo
check.why: The Kodokan began in a small space at the Eishō-ji temple in Tokyo in 1882.

check.q: Before sports used it, what did the word dojo name?
check.why: Buddhist writers used dojo for the place of the Buddha's awakening and later for temple halls.

lessons.title: Dojang and Gymnasium
lessons.mainIdea: Dojang is the Korean word for a training hall, and gym comes from an ancient Greek word.
reading: A taekwondo school often calls itself a *dojang*. That is the Korean word for a training hall. It is written with the same two Chinese characters as the Japanese word dojo, read the Korean way. The name taekwondo itself was chosen in South Korea in the mid-1950s.

The world headquarters of taekwondo is the *Kukkiwon* in Seoul, South Korea. It opened in 1972. The Kukkiwon issues black belt certificates to students in many countries. Many U.S. dojangs were opened by Korean immigrants who arrived after the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 widened entry from Asia.

The word gym is short for *gymnasium*. It comes from the ancient Greek gymnasion, a public place for exercise and study. Its root, gymnos, meant "unclothed," because Greek athletes trained that way. A boxing gym in Illinois carries a name about 2,500 years old.

words.d: the Korean word for a training hall, used by taekwondo schools
the world headquarters of taekwondo in Seoul, South Korea, opened in 1972
a room or building for exercise; from the ancient Greek gymnasion

look.title: Two Flags on a Wall
look.text: In many U.S. taekwondo schools, the flag of South Korea hangs next to the flag of the United States. Ranks are named in Korean. The students come from many backgrounds, and most of them speak English at home.
look.prompt: What does this wall tell a visitor about where the art came from and where it lives now?

check.q: What is a dojang?
choices: the Korean word for a training hall
check.why: Dojang is the Korean word for a training hall, used in taekwondo.

check.q: When did the Kukkiwon open in Seoul?
check.why: The Kukkiwon, the world headquarters of taekwondo, opened in 1972.

check.q: Where does the word gym come from?
choices: an Old English word for rope
check.why: Gym is short for gymnasium, from the Greek gymnasion.

lessons.title: Kwoon, Club and Academy
lessons.mainIdea: Chinese martial arts schools often use the Cantonese word kwoon, while other schools choose club or academy.
reading: Many Chinese martial arts schools in North America call themselves a *kwoon*. Kwoon is the Cantonese way to say guan, a word for a hall or building. Cantonese is spoken in Guangdong province and Hong Kong. Most early Chinese immigrants to the United States came from Guangdong, so Cantonese words spread first.

Bruce Lee was born in San Francisco in 1940 and grew up in Hong Kong. He came back to the United States as a young man and taught in the 1960s. He opened schools in Seattle and Oakland. Chinese American teachers in many cities ran schools long before and after him.

Other schools use words from Europe. A *club* is a group run by its members, often with dues and elected officers. The Budokwai in London, founded in 1918, is one of the oldest judo clubs in Europe. Many Brazilian jiu-jitsu schools use academia, the Portuguese word for academy.

words.d: the Cantonese word for a hall; used by many Chinese martial arts schools
a group run by its own members, who usually pay dues and elect leaders

look.title: Five Names, One Idea
look.text: Dojo comes from Japanese. Dojang comes from Korean. Kwoon comes from Cantonese. Academia comes from Portuguese. Gym comes from ancient Greek. All five name a room where people train together.
look.prompt: Choose one name. Which language and which place does it point back to?

check.q: Why are Cantonese words common in older U.S. Chinese martial arts schools?
choices: Cantonese is the language of Beijing
Most early Chinese immigrants to the U.S. came from Guangdong
check.why: Early Chinese immigrants came mostly from Guangdong, where Cantonese is spoken.

check.q: Which judo club was founded in London in 1918?
check.why: The Budokwai, founded in London in 1918, is one of Europe's oldest judo clubs.

check.q: What is a club?
choices: a group run by its members, who pay dues
a school owned by the state
a room with a raised ring
check.why: A club is run by its own members, who usually pay dues and elect leaders.

lessons.title: The School Wrestling Room
lessons.mainIdea: A high school wrestling room is a public school space run under a state association and a national rule book.
reading: Most Illinois high schools with a team have a *wrestling room*. It is often a plain room covered wall to wall with padded mats. Public money helps build and run it, and any enrolled student may try out. The team competes in *folkstyle* wrestling, the style used in U.S. high schools and colleges.

Folkstyle differs from the two Olympic styles, freestyle and Greco-Roman. Each style has its own scoring rules. U.S. college wrestlers held their first NCAA championships in 1928. Illinois high school boys held their first state championships in 1937, run by the Illinois High School Association, or IHSA.

The rules come from the National Federation of State High School Associations, known as the *NFHS*. It was founded in Chicago in 1920. Its wrestling rule book sets the weight classes, match length and uniforms. In high school wrestling, the heaviest weight class tops out at 285 pounds.

words.d: a school room covered with mats where a wrestling team trains
the style of wrestling used in U.S. high schools and colleges
the National Federation of State High School Associations; it writes rule books for high school sports

look.title: The High School Rule Book
look.text: The book lists the weight classes, the size of the mat, what wrestlers wear, how long a match lasts and how referees award points. State associations that belong to the NFHS use it for their high school meets.
look.cite: NFHS Wrestling Rules Book, published each season by the National Federation of State High School Associations
look.prompt: Why would high schools across the country want to share one rule book?

check.q: What is folkstyle wrestling?
choices: the only style at the Olympics
the style used in U.S. high schools and colleges
a Japanese style from the Kodokan
a style with no weight classes
check.why: Folkstyle is the style of U.S. high schools and colleges; the Olympics use freestyle and Greco-Roman.

check.q: Where was the NFHS founded in 1920?
check.why: The NFHS was founded in Chicago in 1920.

check.q: When did Illinois high school boys hold their first state wrestling championships?
check.why: The IHSA crowned its first boys state wrestling champions in 1937.

lessons.title: Karate in a Storefront
lessons.mainIdea: Karate came to U.S. storefronts after World War II, often carried home by veterans who had served in Asia.
reading: Karate grew on Okinawa, once the center of the *Ryukyu Kingdom*. Japan made the islands a prefecture in 1879. In the early 1900s, Okinawan teachers brought karate into local schools and then to mainland Japan. Funakoshi Gichin gave a well-known demonstration in Tokyo in 1922.

After World War II, U.S. troops were stationed on Okinawa and in Japan. Some trained in local karate halls. When they came home, a few opened schools of their own. Robert Trias, a Navy veteran, opened a karate school in Phoenix, Arizona, in 1946; it is often named as the first on the U.S. mainland.

Many karate schools rent a *storefront*, a shop with a window on a street or strip mall. The owner pays rent and charges monthly *tuition*, a fee for classes. The IHSA does not run karate. Each Illinois karate school follows its style's organization or sets its own ranks and rules.

words.d: the island kingdom centered on Okinawa, made part of Japan in 1879
a rented shop with a window facing a street or parking lot
a fee paid for classes

look.title: Reading a Shop Window
look.text: A storefront window shows a class schedule: young children at 4:30, teens at 5:30, adults at 7:00. A poster announces a belt test on Saturday. A sign says the first class is free. Taped low on the glass is a photo of the school's founder beside his own teacher.
look.prompt: What does this window tell you about how a storefront school pays its rent and shows where it came from?

check.q: Where did karate grow before it reached mainland Japan?
choices: Okinawa, in the old Ryukyu Kingdom
check.why: Karate grew on Okinawa, the center of the Ryukyu Kingdom.

check.q: When did Japan make the Ryukyu Islands a prefecture?
check.why: Japan made the islands Okinawa Prefecture in 1879.

check.q: What does a storefront school charge for classes?
check.why: Storefront schools charge tuition, a fee for classes, to pay rent and teachers.

lessons.title: Judo on a College Campus
lessons.mainIdea: College judo in the U.S. grew in student clubs, with San Jose State as a well-known center.
reading: Kanō Jigorō was an educator who wanted judo taught in schools. Japanese immigrants started judo clubs in Hawaii and on the U.S. West Coast in the early 1900s. Some clubs met in community halls or Buddhist temples. They taught children of the community and later welcomed others.

During World War II, the U.S. government forced about 120,000 Japanese Americans into camps. This *incarceration* closed many West Coast judo clubs. At San Jose State in California, Yosh Uchida had begun coaching judo in 1940, while still a student. After the war he built the school into a top college judo program.

Judo joined the Olympics at Tokyo in 1964. Uchida coached the first U.S. Olympic judo team there. At most U.S. colleges, judo is a *club sport*. Students run the club and pay dues, and the NCAA does not hold a judo championship.

words.d: being locked up; in U.S. history, the forced removal of Japanese Americans to camps in World War II
a college sport run by students, not by the athletic department

look.title: A Campus Flyer
look.text: A flyer on a college bulletin board reads: "Judo Club. Mondays and Thursdays, 7 p.m., Rec Center Room B. All levels welcome. Dues: $30 per semester. Officers elected each spring."
look.prompt: How can you tell from the flyer that this is a club sport and not a varsity team?

check.q: What closed many West Coast judo clubs during World War II?
choices: the forced incarceration of Japanese Americans
check.why: About 120,000 Japanese Americans were forced into camps, which closed many clubs.

check.q: Who coached the first U.S. Olympic judo team in 1964?
check.why: Yosh Uchida of San Jose State coached the first U.S. Olympic judo team.

check.q: How is judo usually run at U.S. colleges?
choices: as a club sport run by students
check.why: At most colleges, judo is a club sport; the NCAA holds no judo championship.

lessons.title: The Boxing Gym
lessons.mainIdea: A boxing gym is built around a ring, and its rules trace back to the Queensberry Rules of 1867.
reading: A boxing gym is easy to spot. A raised *ring*, a square platform with ropes, stands in the room. The name ring is older than the square shape. Early English prize fights took place inside a circle of standing spectators.

Modern boxing rules began with the *Queensberry Rules*, published in London in 1867. John Graham Chambers wrote them. They carry the name of the Marquess of Queensberry, who backed them. The rules called for padded gloves and rounds of three minutes, with one minute of rest between.

Boxing has two worlds. *Amateur* boxers are not paid; USA Boxing, based in Colorado Springs, runs their events and helps pick Olympic teams. Professional boxers fight for money. Illinois law requires professional boxers to hold a state license.

words.d: the raised square platform with ropes where a boxing match takes place
boxing rules published in London in 1867 that required gloves and timed rounds
an athlete who competes without being paid

look.title: The First Rule of 1867
look.text: Rule 1 calls for a fair stand-up boxing match in a 24-foot ring, or as near that size as can be managed.
look.cite: The Queensberry Rules, London, 1867, written by John Graham Chambers
look.prompt: What does the first rule say about the size of the space?

check.q: Who wrote the Queensberry Rules?
check.why: John Graham Chambers wrote them; the Marquess of Queensberry backed them and gave his name.

check.q: What is an amateur boxer?
choices: a boxer who has never won
a boxer with a state pro license
a boxer who competes without pay
check.why: An amateur competes without being paid; USA Boxing runs amateur events.

check.q: Why is a square boxing platform called a ring?
choices: Early prize fights took place inside a circle of spectators
The Queensberry Rules required a round floor
Rings were first used in wrestling rooms
check.why: The name is older than the square; early fights happened inside a ring of onlookers.

lessons.title: Who Writes the Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Each room on the strip answers to a different rule maker, from a state association to a world federation.
reading: The high school wrestling room follows two bodies. The NFHS writes the rule book. The IHSA, founded in 1900, runs the Illinois state series and decides which schools compete in which class. Both are groups of schools, not private businesses.

Judo answers to the *International Judo Federation*, or IJF, founded in 1951. It writes the rules used at the Olympics and world championships. In the United States, USA Judo is the national body. Taekwondo's world body began in 1973 as the World Taekwondo Federation and is now called World Taekwondo.

Karate has many rule makers. Each style, such as Shotokan or Gōjū-ryū, may have its own organizations. The World Karate Federation writes rules for sport karate, which appeared at the Tokyo Olympics held in 2021. A *governing body* is the group that makes the rules and runs the official events for a sport.

words.d: the world governing body of judo, founded in 1951
a group that makes the rules and runs official events for a sport

look.cite: Founding records of the Kodokan, IHSA, NFHS, IJF, Kukkiwon and World Taekwondo

check.q: What is a governing body?
choices: a group that makes the rules and runs official events
a person who owns a storefront
the floor of a wrestling room
check.why: A governing body makes a sport's rules and runs its official events.

check.q: When was the International Judo Federation founded?
check.why: The IJF, judo's world body, was founded in 1951.

check.q: How does karate differ from high school wrestling in who makes the rules?
choices: Karate has one world rule book and wrestling has none
Karate has many style organizations, while school wrestling follows the NFHS
Both are run by the IHSA
check.why: Karate styles have their own organizations; high school wrestling follows the NFHS rule book.

lessons.title: Belts, Records and Brackets
lessons.mainIdea: Belt arts show progress with ranks, while wrestling and boxing show it with records and tournament results.
reading: Kanō Jigorō created a ranking system for judo in the 1880s. Beginners held *kyu* grades. Advanced students earned *dan* grades, and dan holders wore a black belt. Karate teachers in mainland Japan took up the same kyu and dan system in the 1920s.

Taekwondo uses colored belts and black belt dan ranks too. A Kukkiwon certificate records a student's dan rank and can be checked in its records. Colored belts below black vary from school to school. A belt rank belongs to one art and often to one organization.

Wrestling and boxing do not use belts. A wrestler's progress shows in a *record*, the count of wins and losses, and in the state tournament bracket. A boxer also builds a record, match by match. A trophy or a medal marks a result on one day, while a belt marks a rank that stays.

words.d: a grade below black belt in judo and karate
a black belt rank; first dan is the first black belt level
the count of an athlete's wins and losses

look.title: Two Walls
look.text: In the dojo, one wall holds a row of photos of students who earned black belts, each with a date. In the high school wrestling room, one wall holds a painted list of state qualifiers and state medalists, each with a year and a weight class.
look.prompt: What does each wall honor, and how are the two kinds of honor different?

check.q: Who created the kyu and dan ranks for judo?
check.why: Kanō Jigorō created judo's kyu and dan system in the 1880s.

check.q: What is a wrestler's record?
choices: the color of the wrestler's belt
the room where the team trains
the count of wins and losses
check.why: A record counts an athlete's wins and losses.

check.q: When did karate teachers in mainland Japan take up kyu and dan ranks?
check.why: Karate adopted judo's kyu and dan system in mainland Japan in the 1920s.

lessons.title: Paying for the Room
lessons.mainIdea: Who pays for a training room shapes who can walk in, from public school budgets to monthly tuition.
reading: The high school wrestling room is paid for mostly by a public school district. Illinois school districts are funded largely by local property taxes, with state and federal money added. Students on the team do not pay tuition to use the room. Families may still pay for shoes, camps or travel.

A storefront dojo or dojang is a small business. Its owner pays rent, insurance and teachers from monthly tuition and test fees. If families stop paying, the school closes. Some storefront owners also run summer camps or after-school pickup to stay open.

Some boxing gyms are set up as *nonprofits*, organizations that put their money back into their programs. Under federal tax law, many can accept donations that givers deduct from their taxes. Public park districts, which Illinois towns fund through taxes, also host boxing and martial arts classes at low cost.

words.d: a local tax on land and buildings; it pays for much of public schooling in Illinois
an organization that uses its money for its programs, not to make owners rich

look.title: Three Price Tags
look.text: The school wrestling team asks families to buy wrestling shoes. The karate storefront charges a monthly fee plus a fee for each belt test. The park district boxing class charges a small fee for a ten-week session and offers help for families who need it.
look.prompt: Which room is easiest for a new family to try, and what paid for that room?

check.q: What pays for most of a public high school wrestling room in Illinois?
choices: public school funds, largely from property taxes
check.why: Illinois school districts are funded largely by local property taxes, with state and federal help.

check.q: What is a nonprofit?
choices: a group that uses its money for its programs
a business that never charges fees
a school run by the IHSA
check.why: A nonprofit puts its money back into its programs instead of paying owners a profit.

check.q: What happens to a storefront school if families stop paying tuition?
choices: it cannot pay rent and may close
check.why: A storefront is a small business that depends on tuition to pay rent and teachers.

lessons.title: Who Could Walk In
lessons.mainIdea: The doors of these rooms opened to women and to athletes with disabilities over many decades, often after long campaigns.
reading: In 1959, Rena "Rusty" Kanokogi of Brooklyn, New York, won a YMCA judo tournament. Officials took her medal away because she was a woman. She spent the next decades pushing for women's judo. The first women's world judo championships were held in New York in 1980.

Women's judo became an Olympic medal sport at Barcelona in 1992. Women's taekwondo arrived with the sport's first medal events at Sydney in 2000. Women's freestyle wrestling followed in 2004 at Athens. Women's boxing joined at London in 2012.

Judo entered the *Paralympic Games* at Seoul in 1988 for athletes who are blind or have low vision. Women's events were added in 2004. The Paralympics are held in the same city as the Olympics, soon after them. Each step opened a room that had been closed to someone.

words.d: the international games for athletes with disabilities, held after each Olympics
an event where Olympic medals are awarded, not just a demonstration

check.why: Officials took back her medal because she was a woman, and she then campaigned for women's judo.

check.q: When did women's boxing join the Olympics?
check.why: Women's boxing first appeared as an Olympic medal event at London in 2012.

check.q: When did judo enter the Paralympic Games?
check.why: Judo joined the Paralympics at Seoul in 1988 for athletes who are blind or have low vision.

review.q: Where did Robert Trias open a karate school in 1946?
